extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy of science, logic, and foundations of mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and standards for judging scientific and mathematical reasoning: the role of syllogistic premises (major/minor), the epistemic status of axioms and hypotheses, and the inductive grounding of geometrical and mechanical truths.

rubrics_metrics.name: General and particular assertions justified by same evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: “Both assertions are proved together, by the same evidence, namely, the grounds of experience on which the general assertion was made.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When we infer a general proposition (e.g. 'All men are mortal') and then apply it to a particular (Socrates), the particular is not proved by the general alone; both the general and the particular claim rest on the same experiential grounds. The general formula serves as an interpretation of prior experience rather than as an independently established proof of particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of the minor premise
rubrics_metrics.description: “To show that this comparison has been made, is the office of the minor... The minor then identifies the precise kind of likeness possessed by Socrates, as being the kind required by the formula.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The minor premise functions to indicate that a particular has the specific likeness (or marks) required by the generalization. It is primarily a marker that the necessary comparison between the individual and the class-defining marks has been performed; it is a precautionary and interpretative device rather than an independent source of support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syllogistic premises are not necessary conditions of reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: “Reasoning can be carried on without either the one or the other. They are not the conditions of reasoning, but a precaution against erroneous reasoning.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The formal major and minor of a syllogism are convenient expressions that refine and clarify inferences drawn from particulars, but they do not constitute the essential conditions of reasoning. Informal inferences from case to case may be legitimate even when not cast into syllogistic form; syllogistic premises are primarily to make the inference safer and more explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometrical axioms derive from experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Geometrical axioms are generalizations from experience and are not purely a priori self-evidences; they ‘carry their inductive origin on the face of their enunciation.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Axioms like ‘two straight lines cannot inclose a space’ are justified by accumulated, familiar observation and mental experience. The apparent necessity of such axioms arises because experience constantly suggests them, and their simplicity and ubiquity secure implicit assent across minds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by approximation (Method of Concomitant Variations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Though we have no perfectly literal instances (e.g. absolutely straight lines), ‘‘proof by approximation’… the straight line of the definition is the ideal limit... The inference that if they had no breadth or flexure at all, they would inclose no space at all, is a correct inductive inference... conformable to ... the Method of Concomitant Variations.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When idealized mathematical objects do not literally appear in experience, we justify axioms by observing a continuous series of approximations in which the relevant property approaches the ideal. Mathematical limits and concomitant variations supply the inductive bridge from approximate empirical instances to idealized axiomatic claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypotheses as idealized assumptions (in geometry and science)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The hypotheses spoken of in the text are of a different character; they are known not to be literally true, while as much of them as is true is not hypothetical, but certain.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In scientific and geometric reasoning certain hypotheses are acknowledged idealizations—known not to be literally true—but still useful because those parts of them that correspond to experience are certain. One must recognize when a hypothesis is a mere convenient fiction (idealization) versus when it posits a factual agent or entity that can be true or false.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axioms of mechanics are inductively collected from observation
rubrics_metrics.description: “As we admit no such propositions, other than as truths inductively collected from observation, even in geometry itself... let us take one of these axioms and examine its evidence: for instance, that equal forces perpendicularly applied at the opposite ends of equal arms of a straight lever will balance each other.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanics’ fundamental axioms (e.g. lever balance, pressure summation) are not purely self-evident truths but summaries of repeated observation. Their acceptance rests on an abundance of experiential verification rather than on a priori demonstration; examples and appeals to how often we observe the regularity ground their plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessary universal truths must verify themselves in every instance
rubrics_metrics.description: “A truth, necessary and universal, relative to any object of our knowledge, must verify itself in every instance where that object is before our contemplation... The sentiment of such a truth cannot, therefore, but be present to our minds whenever that object is contemplated.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To qualify as necessary and universal, a proposition should be immediately recognizable and confirmed on every occasion of contemplating the relevant object. Such truths form part of the mental picture of the object and so are inseparable from its conception—violations of axioms render the concept incoherent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental images can serve as experimental evidence when precise
rubrics_metrics.description: “We may, and continually do, study nature in our recollections... every body has a perfectly distinct mental image of a straight line, a circle, or a rectangle... we may examine his mental pictures, and find there a property of the outward objects.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In domains where internal representations are vivid and reliable (notably simple geometrical forms), recollection and imagination can function as a basis for judgment and experiment when actual objects are absent. The reliability of such mental evidence varies with the vividness and precision of the recollection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish descriptions from hypotheses; multiple explanations may be consistent
rubrics_metrics.description: Different descriptions and different explanations of a phenomenon may all be true; a hypothesis that merely represents facts (a Description) can be reconcilable with another theory, whereas a hypothesis that posits a material agent (e.g. vortices) may be true or false and contradict another if it asserts incompatible facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing rival theories, determine whether they are merely different descriptive renderings of the same factual behavior (potentially compatible) or positive claims about distinct causal agents (potentially incompatible). Be attentive to the part of a theory that is descriptive device versus factual claim about reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction includes practical inferences, not only scientific generalizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Mill rejects the restriction of 'induction' to cases where a general truth is consciously apprehended for science; many practical inferences from experience (drawn without explicit generalization) are substantially the same operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rubric for calling an inference ‘inductive’ should encompass both explicit scientific generalizations and the everyday case-to-case inferences people use for practical guidance, provided both rest on experience-based generalization even if not formally recorded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Location of fallibility in reasoning (first step versus length)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mill: even if a fundamental axiom is fallible, the risk of error is incurred at the very first step of the reasoning and is not added to by subsequent repetitions of the same axiom; Spencer’s claim that longer heterogeneous arguments increase the test-risk conflates fallibility of premises with error in the reasoning process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating the reliability of a long chain of reasoning, distinguish two sources of fallibility: (1) the initial acceptance of a possibly fallible premise (which determines the primary risk), and (2) additional accidental errors (carelessness, ambiguous terms) introduced by longer trains of thought. The latter are practical hazards, but do not amount to an incremental epistemic weakening of the repeated axiom itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceiving versus believing: conceptual clarity matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Mill notes that changing from 'conceive myself looking into darkness' to 'conceive that I am then and there looking into darkness' marks a transition from conception to belief, implying different uses of 'conceive'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In philosophical and scientific argumentation be precise about whether one is describing imaginative conception or asserting belief; conflating the two can misrepresent what can be known or shown to be possible and affects how evidence and conceivability are used in argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syllogistic formulation as a revisionary safeguard
rubrics_metrics.description: “When we conclude from personal experience without referring to any record ... we do not use, in our thoughts, either a major or a minor, such as the syllogism puts into words. When, however, we revise this rough inference from particulars to particulars, and substitute a careful one, the revision consists in selecting two syllogistic premises. But this neither alters nor adds to the evidence we had before; it only puts us in a better position for judging whether our inference ... is well grounded.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formulating informal inferences as explicit syllogisms is a methodological corrective: it does not provide new evidence but clarifies and tests the adequacy of the original inference. Use syllogistic reconstruction as a diagnostic and justificatory tool rather than as the source of evidential force.
